passage:
People think we decided on some romantic night. We didn't. We decided in the worst week of Gurpreet's life.
His father's shop flooded in the rains, and Gurpreet spent five days hauling wet stock and arguing on the phone. He was short-tempered and exhausted, and once he snapped at me over nothing. An hour later he came back and said, "That was unfair. I'm sorry. I'm scared." That mattered to me more than any gift.
He'd seen me at my worst too, the semester I failed stats and cried at his cousin's wedding.
So one night on the hostel steps, we talked properly. I want to do a master's in Delhi; he wants to take over the shop in Amritsar. We didn't pretend that away. We made a plan for two years apart and a date to review it.
Then I said, "I choose this. With my eyes open." And he said, "Me too." That's Madhuri's great romance.

qa.q: What happened to Gurpreet's father's shop?
qa.a: His father's shop flooded in the rains.

qa.q: Why did Gurpreet's apology matter so much to Madhuri?
qa.a: It showed that under stress Gurpreet could own his mistakes and be honest about fear, which told Madhuri more than any gift.

qa.q: What makes this commitment grounded rather than just a feeling?
qa.a: They had seen each other in hard times, talked openly about clashing goals, and made a plan with a review date before choosing each other.

qa.q: How might Gurpreet have felt hearing 'I choose this. With my eyes open'?
qa.a: Gurpreet likely felt trusted and steady, knowing Madhuri chose him after seeing his worst week, not just his good days.

grounding: Shows a couple committing after seeing each other under stress and speaking honestly about goals, as a clear-eyed decision.

passage:
I've been Mehak's roommate for three years, so I've seen her with Irfan through most of it. The first months were all giggles on the phone and roses on Valentine's Day. Cute, but I didn't think much of it.
What changed my mind was last winter. Mehak's mother was in hospital for weeks, and Irfan sat in that hospital corridor every evening after his internship, with food, and just listened. When he lost his placement offer in March, Mehak didn't give him a speech. She helped him redo his CV at 2 a.m.
Last month I heard them on our balcony talking about jobs, cities, money, even how many years before marriage. Serious, calm voices. No roses.
Then Mehak came in and said, "We've decided. We're committed." She didn't look dreamy. She looked certain. I can't know everything they feel, but to me, Sonali, it looked like a choice they'd made together.

qa.q: Where did Irfan sit every evening while Mehak's mother was in hospital?
qa.a: Irfan sat in that hospital corridor every evening after his internship.

qa.q: What does Mehak's certain, not dreamy, look suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Mehak made a clear-eyed decision, not a swept-away feeling, after seeing Irfan in hard times.

qa.q: What helped this couple reach a grounded commitment?
qa.a: They supported each other through real stress, like the hospital weeks and the lost placement, and then talked honestly about jobs, cities and money.

qa.q: How has Sonali's view of the couple changed over three years?
qa.a: Sonali first saw giggles and roses and didn't think much of it; after watching them through hard times, Sonali saw a real choice made together.

grounding: Illustrates, through a roommate's eyes, a couple committing after seeing each other in stress and joy and talking honestly about goals.

passage:
March. Swati and Anjali had been together for a year, mostly the happy parts: weekend trips, late breakfasts. Then Swati's father was admitted to hospital with a heart problem, and Anjali took leave from her internship to sit with her in the corridor for three days, bringing tea and making the calls Swati couldn't face.

May, two months on. Anjali failed her licensing exam. She shut herself in and snapped at Swati for asking how she was. Swati stayed anyway, and on the third day Anjali cried and apologised.

August. On the rooftop, they had the talk they'd been circling. Swati wanted to go abroad for a PhD. Anjali wanted to stay near her family. They talked for hours.

"I want to be with you," Swati said at the end. "Not because it feels nice. Because I've seen you at your worst, and I still choose you."

Anjali held her hand. "Same. Eyes open."

qa.q: How many days did Anjali sit with Swati in the hospital corridor?
qa.a: Three days.

qa.q: What does Swati mean when she says she chooses Anjali "not because it feels nice"?
qa.a: She feels a deep, calm certainty; after seeing Anjali at her worst, her commitment is a clear choice rather than just a feeling.

qa.q: What makes this commitment grounded?
qa.a: They have seen each other in stress as well as joy, and they speak honestly about different goals before committing.

qa.q: How might Anjali feel when Swati stays despite the snapping?
qa.a: She probably feels ashamed at first, then relieved and loved, which is why she cries and apologises.

grounding: Swati and Anjali see each other through a parent's illness and a failed exam, talk honestly about goals, and commit with open eyes.

passage:
Parveen, you ask how I knew your Phuphi was the one. Your Nitin uncle will tell you, but it's not a love story from the films.

We'd been courting for two years when her mother fell very ill. For six months, Rukhsana ran the house, cared for her mother, and still finished her exams. I saw her exhausted, snappish, crying in the kitchen at midnight. And I saw her pick herself up every morning.

She saw me too. When I lost my first job, she didn't pity me. She sat me down with a list of places to apply.

After all that, we sat on the ghats one evening and talked about everything: where we'd live, whether she'd work, how many children, how we'd care for our parents. It took three evenings.

Then I asked her. Not because I was swept away. Because I'd seen her in the worst times, and I chose her anyway. That was the turning point.

qa.q: How long had Nitin and Rukhsana been courting when her mother fell ill?
qa.a: Two years.

qa.q: How did Rukhsana feel during the six months of her mother's illness?
qa.a: She was exhausted and at times overwhelmed, crying in the kitchen at midnight, but determined to pick herself up.

qa.q: What turning point in the story made the commitment grounded?
qa.a: The three evenings on the ghats talking openly about goals, after they had seen each other through hard times.

qa.q: How might Rukhsana have felt when Nitin lost his first job?
qa.a: She may have been concerned but practical and supportive, wanting to help rather than pity him.

grounding: Nitin uncle recalls committing to Rukhsana after seeing each other through illness and job loss and talking honestly about goals, commitment as an open-eyed choice.

passage:
The flat in Bengaluru had no power for the third day in a row, and Kunal and Rhea were both working from home with laptop batteries dying and deadlines landing.

By evening they were short with each other. Rhea snapped when Kunal took the last charged power bank. He apologised, then went and borrowed a neighbour's inverter socket for her laptop.

Later, by candlelight, eating cold sandwiches, Rhea said, "We've seen each other at our best. This week we've seen each other at our worst."

"And?" Kunal said.

"And I still want to marry you. But we need to talk about the things we keep skipping. Your job transfer. My mother living with us."

They talked until the candle burned out. Transfers, mothers, money, children. No big promises, just honest answers.

At midnight Kunal said, "So we're deciding this. Not just feeling it."

"Yes," Rhea said. "Eyes open."

qa.q: How many days had the flat been without power?
qa.a: Three days in a row.

qa.q: What was Rhea feeling when she snapped about the power bank?
qa.a: She was stressed and frustrated, with her deadline landing and her laptop dying.

qa.q: What turned a bad week into a turning point for the couple?
qa.a: They used it to talk honestly about the things they had skipped, like the transfer and her mother, and chose commitment with open eyes.

qa.q: How might Kunal see Rhea's list of hard topics?
qa.a: He may feel a bit nervous but relieved and respected, since they are deciding together instead of just hoping.

grounding: During a stressful power cut, Kunal and Rhea see each other at their worst and speak honestly about goals, choosing commitment with open eyes.

passage: On the balcony of their rented flat in Pune, Rekha set down two glasses of cutting chai and a sheet of paper. "Before we say forever, let's be boring and honest," she said. Shreya laughed, but she took the pen. They had been together two years. Shreya had seen Rekha snap at everyone during her father's surgery, then go back and apologise to each nurse by name. Rekha had seen Shreya lose her job and spend a week in pyjamas before sending out forty applications. They had also danced badly at three weddings. On the paper they wrote: Rekha wants to study abroad in two years. Shreya wants to stay near her mother. How we share rent. Who calls whom first after a fight. They circled the abroad question twice and agreed to decide it together by spring. Then Shreya put the pen down. "I'm choosing you, knowing all of this." Rekha squeezed her hand. "Same. Eyes open."

qa.q: How long had Shreya and Rekha been together?
qa.a: They had been together two years.

qa.q: What does Rekha's suggestion to be 'boring and honest' suggest she wants?
qa.a: She wants their promise to rest on clear, shared facts rather than on the joy of the moment, and she seems calm and secure enough to face hard topics.

qa.q: What makes this a strong moment to commit rather than an impulsive one?
qa.a: They have already seen each other at their worst, during the surgery and the job loss, and they name real goals, even the clash over studying abroad, before deciding.

qa.q: What would change if Shreya had said 'forever' without talking about Rekha's plan to study abroad?
qa.a: The clash with Shreya's wish to stay near her mother would likely surface later as a painful surprise, instead of being something they agreed to work on together.

grounding: Shows a couple committing only after seeing each other through stress and joy and talking honestly about goals.
